What is the essential teaching in 'Kamma: A Study Guide'?

In 'Kamma: A Study Guide', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Kamma Neither Dark nor Bright
The doctrine of kamma (karma — action) is one of the Buddha's central teachings."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

This section teaches: *"§ 1. "Monks, there are these three sectarian guilds that — when cross-examined, pressed for reasons, & rebuked by wise people — even though they may explain otherwise, remain stuck in [a doctrine of] inactivity. Which three?
"There are brahmans & contemplatives who hold this teaching, hold this view: 'Whatever a person experiences — pleasant, painf..."* The core instruction is to turn investigation inward (*opanayiko*) toward what is already present in body, speech, and mind — not to seek the Dhamma outside or in future states. Whatever theme this section addresses, the method is the same: sustained, patient, non-grasping awareness that allows the truth to reveal itself. As Ajahn Mun taught: when the mind sees clearly, there is no longer any need to go looking.

This text mentions suffering (dukkha). Can you explain its role in practice?

In this text, dukkha appears in this context: *"So in this case, Kalamas, don't go by reports, by legends, by traditions, by scripture, by conjecture, by inference, by analogies, by agreement through pondering views, by probability, or by the thoug"* Understanding suffering (dukkha) is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by dukkha into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.

This text describes jhāna and meditation levels. What are the key stages?

The text teaches: *"Quite withdrawn from sensuality, withdrawn from unskillful mental qualities, I entered & remained in the first jhana: rapture & pleasure born from withdrawal, accompanied by directed thought & evaluat"* Three levels of concentration are distinguished: (1) momentary concentration — the mind briefly settles then withdraws; (2) threshold concentration — the mind rests at its underlying level for a sustained time, often accompanied by a nimitta (sign); (3) fixed penetration (appanā samādhi) — full jhāna, where the mind abides in deep stillness endowed with applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and unification. Each level is a stepping stone; none should be forced. Develop mindfulness, and samādhi will arise of its own accord like water finding its level.

Why does the preceptor teach the five meditation themes at ordination?

The text explains: *"Knowledge in terms of stress, knowledge in terms of the origination of stress, knowledge in terms of the cessation of stress, knowledge in terms of the way of practice leading to the cessation of stress: This, monks, is called right view."
§ 22."* The five themes — hair of head (kesā), hair of body (lomā), nails (nakhā), teeth (dantā), skin (taco) — are not arbitrary. They target the root of infatuation with the body. The skin, as the outermost layer, is what we are actually attracted to when we conceive of a body as beautiful. Contemplating the skin as a wrapping that holds together otherwise repulsive components directly undercuts sensual desire. This is the very first teaching given to a new monk — showing that the entire path begins with honest, unflinching investigation of the body.
